subsubtopic: NEED FOR EQUAL PROTECTION FOR ALL AUTOMOBILE PASSENGERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 4,630 Canadian men and women lost their lives in 1985, and 258,000 of our fellow citizens were injured in highway accidents-262,630 road victims altogether. In the same year, 46,333 people died from malignant tumours and 58,331 from heart diseases. The road made more victims than these two illnesses combined.
Considering the money we spend on medical research to save lives, it seems to me that North American car manufacturers could easily install safety belts, an initiative which does not require research since the technology already exists.
Since 1969 European cars makers have been installing shoulder safety belts for rear-seat passengers.
I would urge all Canadian men and women to sign the petition I am circulating so that North American manufacturers will understand that time has come to provide all passengers-front-and rear-seat occupants alike-with the same protection in case of road accidents. The money saved in hospital care could be earmarked for research in and development of cures for heart conditions, cancer and other diseases.

subsubtopic: PERFORMANCE OF ABITIBI-TEMISCAMINGUE REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, August 21, 1987, was a memorable day for the people of Abitibi. About 1,500 people from various towns and villages in the area, as well as from New Quebec, applauded the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) and his wife Mila, the Ministers from Quebec and Conservative Members at Saint-Sauveur Church
Community Hall in Val-d'Or, where everyone was invited to a corn roast.
The Prime Minister praised the Abitibi-Temiscamingue region's record for the lowest unemployment rate in Quebec: 6.9 per cent compared with 18.6 per cent in 1984.
The Prime Minister and Mrs. Mulroney signed the City of Val-d'Or's guest book at the request of the Mayor, Mr. Andre Pelletier, in the presence of the aldermen. On the same occasion, the President of the CRDAT provided information on the most pressing problems affecting Abitibi-Temiscamingue.
Mr. Speaker, our region has deserved the attention it has received from a Conservative Government and it will continue to receive that attention with Brian Mulroney as Prime Minister of Canada.
This is a Government that listens to the people.

subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA TROLLER FLEET-SALMON CATCH ALLOCATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) has praised the troll fleet in the Gulf of Georgia because it can be selective in the species of salmon that it harvests. He has said that it should be maintained. But his actions speak louder than his words.
This year's allocation of salmon was set below the minimum needed for many trollers to survive. Now, to add insult to injury, trollers are being shut down before they have been able to catch even this quota. In the meantime, other gear types are being allowed to fish for a good sockeye run. Trollers see this as rank discrimination that has nothing whatever to do with conservation.
In the interests of maintaining this small but vital section of our Pacific fishery I call upon the Minister to take a second look at the situation and to ensure sufficient allocation of fish and sufficient days' fishing so that the Gulf trollers can survive.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-ECONOMIC COUNCIL'S PROJECTION OF BENEFITS
CANADA-UNITED STATES NEGOTIATIONS-ECONOMIC COUNCIL'S PROJECTION OF BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hardly a day goes by that a senior citizen on a fixed income does not complain to me about the high cost of living. Understandably, they do not believe the inflation statistics when they see prices increasing each week at the supermarket. Because of that seniors in my riding, and seniors all across the country, should take a careful look at the new study by the Economic Council of Canada which states that consumers would be the first to win from free trade with the United States. Lower import prices would give them more to spend.
The Economic Council of Canada has good news for Canadian workers as well. According to its report, free trade with the United States would create at least 189,000 new jobs, and possibly as many as 350,000. The manufacturing sector alone would gain 42,000 jobs.
The study goes on to state that free trade would stimulate our economy fairly and evenly across the country but, because of their size, Quebec and Ontario would net about 60 per cent of the economic benefits.
Let us hope that the CBC will inform Canadian seniors and workers about this new study instead of ignoring it as it has done up until now.

I have observed many occasions on which the CBC has conveniently and with ulterior motives either ignored or exaggerated issues in a conscious effort to promote its socialist beliefs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said on the resumption of Parliament for this so-called emergency session, it is clear the real reason we were called back, only for the thirteenth time since Confederation, has nothing to do with the refugee situation. It has everything to do with the absolutely obscene desire of the Government of Canada to bow to American pressure to amend our drug patent legislation and dramatically raise drug prices in order to maintain the free trade negotiations with the U.S. That is the reason and it is a cop-out, as well as a cave-in to the American pharmaceutical industry and the U.S. trade negotiations.

It is indisputable that Bill C-22 before the House, as introduced by the Government, will increase by several hundred million dollars a year the prices paid by Canadian men and women for their medicinal drugs. That is an indisputable fact. No matter what the Government and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (M. Andre) may say, they cannot change that fact. Well, as we could have expected, the Government is trying to have us believe that the prices will not increase, while we all very well know that they will.

Does the Government really think that Canadians were not listening when the leading authority on this issue, Dr. Harry Eastman, stated repeatedly that there is no doubt whatsoever in his mind that drug prices will rise as a result of this Bill?
Patent Act
Let me quote from his November, 1986, interview on CBC's As It Happens. Dr. Eastman had this to say:
The entry of generics which push down prices would be somewhat delayed
and therefore the average prices would be higher than they would be under the
present legislation.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) says that is not true. When pressed he repeatedly makes an argument that what we contend is very narrow and highly misleading. He says that under his Bill the cost of new brand name drugs will not be higher than they are now when they first come on the market. His argument is that if last year someone invented a new brand of pain-killer and brought it on the market at $5 a bottle, then invented another brand the following year and brought it on at $5 a bottle, and so on, there is no increase in price. However, when we talk about increased prices we are not just talking about the initial market price of brand-name drugs, we are talking about the total cost of drugs to Canadians. If a generic manufacturer can make the same kind of pain-killer and sell it for $1 a bottle instead of $5, that means the consumer pays less. That is what is at issue herd.
Under this Bill the generic manufacturer will not have the opportunity to produce a drug and sell it to Canadians for seven to 10 years. The consumer will have to pay the higher price for the brand name product until that period elapses. Yet the Minister continues to say that giving patent protection of seven to 10 years, which prohibits the manufacture and sale of cheaper generic drugs during that period, will not increase drug prices. That just does not hold up.

The Minister claims also that the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board, provided for under this Bill, will prevent prices from increasing. But how will it achieve that? The Board will only have the power to set prices which are reasonable and in line with international prices. Well, just now, our prices are generally lower than international prices; for instance, they are two to five times lower than those paid in the United States. With such a criterion in the Bill, it is more than likely that the prices will increase instead of coming down. Moreover, when the time comes for the Board to review the price of a drug developed, say, in the United States or Switzerland, it will not be able to investigate the research costs of this foreign maker. It will have to take the word of pharmaceutical companies, those same companies it has been mandated to monitor.
A number of other studies reached the same conclusion as Dr. Eastman in his report, namely, that extending the duration of the patents will increase the prices of medicinal drugs.
Even the United States trade representative, Clayton Yeutter, has admitted that drug prices will go up. On the CBC's The Journal on November 19, 1986, he said:

August 26, 1987
Patent Act
In some cases maybe this will raise the price at the retail level of some of
these products.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, some estimates put the cost to Canadians of delaying generic competition at upwards of $5 billion over the 10 years from 1988 to 1997.
An analysis of the various estimates completed in July for the special committee of the Senate on Bill C-22 by the research bureau of the Library of Parliament says that prices will go up. Add to that the Minister's announcement that he intended to provide $100 million to the provinces, originally to cover increased drug prices in the pharmacare and medicare programs but now amended to go to the provinces only if the money is spent on research and development. What was that $100 million for if not as a result of his own anticipation that drug prices will go up?
The Minister says that he has studies which prove that drug prices will not change. We asked him in the House of Commons where those studies are; to produce them and give us the facts. 1 submit that if the Minister had a single scrap of paper to prove his contention that drug prices will not go up he would have plastered it on every billboard in the country. The truth is that he has no such evidence to back up his argument.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The Minister's answer to that is that with longer patent protection there will be more research done in Canada and, therefore, more jobs. He says that is the reason he has brought in this legislation. Let us look at the experience in the United States where brand name drugs are given exclusive monopoly protection for a 17-year period. Their prices are now two to five times as high as Canadian prices.
The New York Times of July 28, a newspaper to which I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) pays close attention after its recent article on him, reports that the head of the Senate Sub-committee on Anti-trust Monopolies and Business Rights is planning hearings this fall on the drug companies' possible anti-trust violations.
U.S. legislators, Congressmen and Senators, have told the brand name manufacturers of the United States that if they do not control their prices more realistically, Congress will consider imposing legislation similar to that which we introduced in Canada in 1969.
It is claimed that higher brand name prices are necessary to fund research and development of new drugs. With regard to that, listen to what representative Harry Waxman, Chairman of the United States Sub-Committee on Health and the Environment, had to say with reference to a study of the 25 largest companies with two-thirds of all prescription drug sales in the United States. This is a quote from the Wall Street Journal of July 20, 1987.
For the years 1982 to 1986 we found that revenue gains due to price
increases were three times greater than their total increase in research and
development expenditures.
We also found that companies spent as much on marketing as they did on research and development. The conclusion is inescapable. The recent price increases are not producing new drugs, they are filling corporate coffers.
if that is what is happening in a jurisdiction with a 17-year monopoly protection, how does the Minister claim he will get research and development in Canada with seven to ten-year protection? The answer is that he is not and he knows he is not.
I have a confidential document produced by our embassy in Washington under what it calls the U.S. Corporate Liaison Program. It is a report on meetings between senior embassy staff in Washington and representatives of the United States industry. One company interviewed was Pfizer Incorporated, one of the largest brand name drug manufacturers in the United States, indeed in the world. This is what the Canadian officials report that the company told them in the course of those discussions.
Firm welcomes proposed Canadian Patent Act amendments but feels they would still fall short of what is called for. Accordingly, it would unlikely make early commitment to significant additional activity in Canada.

The Minister says that 3,000 jobs will be created. The Prime Minister said the same thing yesterday on the Hill before the employees of those pharmaceutical companies. However, according to a study made by the Canadian Drug Manufacturers' Association, the Bill could result in the loss of 9,000 jobs throughout the economy. It would mean a net loss of 6,000 jobs.
He says that under the present rules, the large drug companies do not make any research in Canada but that they will do some if the Bill is passed. How can the Minister say such a thing, say that will happen if his Bill is passed, when he knows full well that even before the 1969 amendments, there was very little research and development work carried out by multinationals in Canada? He even states that he has commitments worth $1,4 billion from drug companies.
However, I have read the Bill. There is no mention of commitments to invest in research. None whatsoever. Those agreements will remain confidential, just like the reviews on which the Minister bases his assertion that prices will not change.
Who is the Minister trying to fool?

Why does the Minister reject the royalty fund proposed by the Senate following the Eastman recommendations? Under that scheme, generics would pay a 14 per cent royalty for the use of brand name discoveries which would be available after four years. The funds would be paid back to the brand name companies for proven research. What better guarantee that money would go back into research for new drugs? The Minister rejects that plan in favour of the United States style system which has been proven ineffective in creating new research and new drugs.
August 26, 1987

One must ask oneself why the multinational companies are spending millions of dollars in a lobbying effort here and in the United States to get this legislation passed. That is not a difficult question to answer. They want to shut out the generic competition because generic competition means less money for them.
When I was the first Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Department having been set up under the Prime Ministership of the late Lester B. Pearson, I had the privilege to begin the process which led to the changes to the Patent Act of 1969 which the current Government is attempting to reverse with this Bill.

We brought in the Act from which the present regulations derive because drug prices in Canada were exorbitant, as they are now becoming in the United States. Our drugs were among the most expensive in the world in 1969. We wanted more competition in this sector in order to bring down prices. We succeeded. Today, our pharmaceutical prices are among the lowest and the most affordable in the world and even the U. S. Department of Health has studied our legislation to see if it would not be worthwhile to adopt similar legislation to lower drug prices in the United States.
It is well worth noting, Madam Speaker, that in 1969, more competition did not bring about less research. In fact, there was an increase in research activity and according to the study done by Dr. Eastman, during 1983, Canadians saved 211 million dollars thanks to competition from generic drugs. The Minister contends that he has another study which shows that, had his bill been in force in 1983, Canadian consumers would have saved almost an equivalent amount. But, then again, he has not made this study public.
One of the Minister's most pathetic arguments in defending this Bill is that Canada is considered an international pirate. He said that we are stealing other people's ideas. He tells us that our current legislation is incompatible with our international treaty obligations. However, Roy Davidson, a former economic adviser in the Minister's own Department, says that is simply not true.
As Dr. Davidson points out, we are not contravening international patent conventions to which we are signatories. Nowhere in that convention does it say that discoverers or inventors are entitled to a monopoly on the production of their invention, as would be the case for 10 years with the Minister's Bill.
Some countries give no patent protection at all. Japan requires foreign firms to co-venture with domestic firms in the marketing of new drug products. Britain and some other European countries rely on centralized purchasing power to regulate both price and industrial benefits. France and
Patent Act
Belgium have strict price controls on pharmaceutical products. Each nation attempts to prevent the exploitation of higher drug prices in its own way and in its own jurisdiction.

In 1969, we opted in Canada for compulsory licensing in order to promote competition. And this is what happened. However, the Minister's Bill would put Canada in a unique position in the world as far as drug prices are concerned. Manufacturers will be under no obligation whatsoever to invest in return for the long term protection they will be getting. They will not have to make additional research and development expenditures. There is no obligation, therefore no guarantee.
During the 40 years before 1969, when the current Act went into force, including when I was in charge as Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, foreign corporations enjoyed the kind of protection provided for under Bill C-22. But no new drugs were produced in Canada in those 40 years.
The simple truth is those international corporations will keep on doing their research in their own countries, as they always did, and the Bill will do nothing more than help them increase their profits on the backs of Canadians by restricting competition.
Such has been the experience before the current Act came into force, and I predict such will be the experience if the legislation is passed by this Parliament.
Madam Speaker, who indeed will benefit from the Bill? Not Canadian consumers, that is for sure, but rather the large multinational corporations in the drugs industry. There is absolutely no doubt about that.
We must ask ourselves this question: Why would multinational companies spend millions of dollars to have this Bill passed, to lobby here and in the United States? The reason is clear, they want to make more money.
As underlined by Dr. Eastman, research and development will probably never amount to much in Canada, given the limited size of our domestic market. Remember that we account for only 2 per cent of the world market.
The Liberal caucus and Party have always supported Dr. Eastman's recommendations. They are positive changes to the present Act designed to encourage research and at the same time alter prices. The recommendations of the Senate are based-through the Liberal amendments proposed in the House-on Dr. Eastman's recommendations and we subscribe to them. We consider it necessary to strike a balance between protection of intellectual property and prices paid by consumers, and we believe that Dr. Eastman did just that in his report.

We have heard a lot of rhetoric from the Prime Minister and various Ministers about how an non-elected Senate is attempting to thwart the will of the people. In one breath, the Prime Minister say, "They have no right whatsoever to change

August 26, 1987
Patent Act
our legislation". Then in the next breath his Minister accepts Senate amendments on the transportation legislation. The Minister for Consumer and Corporate Affairs accepts one amendment in total and two others in modified form. The Government can be selective, accepting some amendments from the Senate, as it is doing in this so-called emergency session, and reject others when it chooses and, in doing so, say that the Senate is not exercising its constitutional prerogative.
The Prime Minister speaks about confrontation between the two Houses. There has been no confrontation between the House and the Senate at all as yet. There have been some very uncharacteristic remarks made in the House about the quality of individual Senators. Such remarks are ordinarily not allowed by the Chair in either Chamber. However, there is no confrontation at the moment. That is sheer hypocrisy. The Senate has exercised its constitutional prerogative to amend a Bill of the House of Commons and send it back here.
The Prime Minister had an opportunity to propose to the Premiers a curb on the Senate's power during his negotiations at Meech Lake. He had the opportunity two years ago to curb the powers of the Senate. 1 debated this issue with the then Minister of Justice on June 7, 1985. The Prime Minister did not proceed with that resolution and there was only one day of debate. We replied on that occasion that we were interested in real Senate reform which would go to the heart of the issue. We wanted an elected Senate to represent the regions of Canada and achieve a better equilibrium from our Confederation.
It is sheer hyprocrisy to suggest that there is confrontation and that a non-democratic House is abusing its role. It is the kind of silly, inflamed rhetoric we hear from the Prime Minister whenever he gets into trouble.
Consider the charade we went through during the last two days about what the Prime Minister wanted to do with the Senate. Yesterday, he was going to abolish it, reform it, elect it. Suddenly, he recognized that he made a deal with the Premiers and did not have that unilateral maneuverability any longer. He had to return to the Premiers to honour his commitment.
Today, I asked him if he will honour that commitment to the Premiers to allow them to appoint, honour his commitment to the House to abolish the Senate, or honour his commitment to the regions of Canada to propose an elected Senate? There is sheer confusion and sheer hypocrisy.
When the Prime Minister proposed that phoney abolition offer two years ago, at that time the provinces had to approve it seven out of ten, with 50 per cent of the population. I knew that and thought it was absolute subterfuge and an absolutely cynical, hollow offer.
When the Prime Minister, in his exasperation and phoney impatience, brought a resolution before the House of Commons, we debated it. We were ready to reform the Senate and adjust an equilibrium in our Confederation. The Prime
Minister did not address the issue, did not attend the House on that day and speak to the issue. The Minister of Justice and 1 each had a one-hour dialogue and that was the limit of the Government's effort to deal with the Senate.
It is a cheap attempt by the Prime Minister to take the focus off this disastrous Bill and to take some shots at the Liberal majority in the Senate. It is a bluff and a smoke-screen designed to draw attention away from this bad legislation.
The issue is not a constitutional one, certainly not yet. The issue is whether this Bill will raise drug prices for Canadians, whether it will really encourage research, or whether it is one of the great shams proposed by the Government against the consumers of Canada. The Prime Minister is as interested in talking about reform of the Senate in substance as he is about talking about the substance of this drug Bill, which is not at all.
When talking about the behaviour of Senators, the Prime Minister used very uncomplimentary language. Let us consider how all those Tory Senators responded when presented with these amendments and recommendations of the Committee in the Upper House. How did they demonstrate their leadership and exercise their role in acting for the Prime Minister and people of Canada on this important legislation? They abstained from voting. They ducked. They did not oppose, they did not propose, they did not vote for, they did not vote against. If I were allowed this language in the House of Commons I would say, "What a derogation of constitutional responsibilities".
Even the New Democratic Party, which advocates the abolition of the Senate, is willing to compromise that longstanding written constitutional position and its Party proposals and, in this case, cheer the Senate on on this particular issue. They agree with us about the merits of this Bill. This Bill simply raises drug prices for Canadians and increases profits for the multinational companies. I commend the NDP for having weighed their two conflicting beliefs against this Bill, against the Senate, coming out in favour of the best interests of all Canadians, which is to amend this Bill in the manner suggested by the Senate, and as suggested by our Party when it was before the House of Commons.
Our position is quite clear on the jurisdiction of the Upper House. We want an elected Senate. We want fundamental reform, but as long as the Senate remains a nominated Chamber, as long as it remains a non-elected Chamber, no matter who appoints them-giving the Premiers the powers of appointment is no significant reform-at the end of the day the elected House of Commons must prevail. That is a clear position of the Liberal Party.
But we have not reached that point, the end of the day. I would urge the Minister to look at a compromise, to look at these amendments once again and consider the arguments that have been made, the study made in the other place and the
August 26, 1987

extensive debate here in the House. 1 urge him to weigh the interests and give intellectual property and patent rights adequate protection, whatever research and development that may bring, but at the same time achieve a balapce and equilibrium for the Canadian consumer, for the aged, the sick, the handicapped and for the four million Canadians who do not enjoy a drug plan, those people who really face the brunt of this legislation.
Why are the recommendations of Dr. Eastman and those of the Senate being rejected? It is for one simple reason. The American multinational drug companies do not like it. An earlier version of this Bill reflected the Eastman report. A summer elapsed and this new Bill was brought in which reflects further discussions with the Americans and the pharmaceutical companies south of the border. It was also brought in to accord the priorities of the American negotiators in the free-trade negotiations. American multinational drug companies are forcing the U.S. administration to make passage of Bill C-22 a condition of the trade talks. The Government has caved in to that pressure. It has been completely spineless. It has changed its original Bill to Bill C-22 in order to accommodate the American pharmaceutical companies and the American trade negotiators. I find it absolutely shameful that this Government and this Prime Minister are willing to sell out our poor, our sick and our disadvantaged just to improve the profit margins of the multinational drug companies.
The Minister says that even if prices go up, it does not really matter because they are all covered by provincial drug plans in any event. What a spurious and deceitful argument. What about the four million Canadians who are not covered by drug plans? What about the millions more who are only partially covered? What about them? "To hell with them", says the Minister. "To hell with Canadian taxpayers who are going to foot the bill to pay either directly for increased drug prices or indirectly through increased taxes to cover the increased cost of drug plans under provincial legislation".
This Government should hang its head in shame when the leading consumer protection advocate in the United States, Ralph Nader, feels obliged to speak across the border and tell the Canadian Government that what it is doing with this Bill will only hurt Canadian consumers and increase profits for the large multinationals. But the Minister and the Prime Minister have repeatedly denied that there is any connection between the trade talks and this legislation, even though the joint communique issued at the Shamrock Summit lists intellectual property as the one of the areas of discussion. Even though the United States trade representative, Clayton Yeutter, lists Canadian drug patent legislation as an irritant which, and I quote from the National Trade Estimate, 1986 report on Foreign Trade Barriers, Office of the United States Trade Representative, at pages 54-55, "costs U.S. pharmaceutical interests significant lost revenues each year".
It also states:
Patent Act
The United States continues to raise its concerns at senior Government
levels. It urges speedy submission of modifying legislation to address serious
U.S. concerns about the inadequacy of Canadian patent protection in this
area.
That was right at the top of the list of irritant^ which the United States wanted to remove as a price fo]t free trade negotiations with the United States.
The President pf the United States in his letter to Senator Packwood, that great "Dear Bob" letter which we have often quoted in the House of Commons, dated May 8, 1986, said: "Dear Bob, thank you again for your forceful efforts in preserving our fast-track proposal for a Canada free trade agreement". Senator Packwood from the State of Oregon came along and voted for the fast-track but he had made a deal.
The last paragraph of the President's letter to the Senator reads: "We fully realize that lumber and other pending trade irritants must be resolved before we submit to the Senate the results of the comprehensive negotiations". Right at the top of that list of irritants is the pharmaceutical industry's demands for this legislation.
How clearer could it be? Yet the Minister and the Prime Minister say there is no connection. That is sheer nonsense. The Parliament of Canada is now in emergency session to meet Washington's timetable. This is the first time a legislature of a sovereign nation was every called into emergency session just to abide by and conform to the wishes of another nation.
The Government can deny it all it wants, but that is the truth, and what a shameful truth it is. Despite the attempts of the Government to hide the facts and cover up its real intentions, and to confuse Canadians on these trade talks, it is now becoming clearer every day that it has been the Government's intention all along to risk Canadian economic, political and cultural sovereignty in return for a free trade deal.
The Americans may be many things but they are not stupid. A Yankee trader is still a good Yankee trader. They know a good thing when they see one, and boy did they see a good thing when this Government got elected and the Prime Minister went down to New York. I am sure we all remember. He put on his black tie and told all those American bankers and investment brokers, "Hi guys. My name is Brian Mul-roney. I am Prime Minister of Canada and I want you to know that Canada is open for business again". The next day he returned to the House of Commons and I said to him, "That is terrific. We are open for business again. I never thought we were closed. We may be open for business again, Prime Minister, but this country is not up for sale", and that is what we are saying to the people of Canada.
Canadians know that the Government wants a free trade deal at any cost. The plan was simple, get the Prime Minister and the President together, put on the black tie, a few handshakes, a few songs, a few limericks, a nice meal, a nice show and that will keep those simple Canadians happy, especially

August 26, 1987
Patent Act
the Prime Minister, who seems to be pretty easily impressed by anything that happens south of the border.
At the same time the U.S. dangled the carrot of a free trade deal in front of the Prime Minister. It put the heavy hitters to work behind closed doors to get everything it wanted before the deal was signed. It wanted to eliminate the National Energy Program, and what it considered to be the restrictive provisions of the Foreign Investment Review Act, before the deal was ever begun, before it was ever signed. The Americans know the Canadian Government is not going to put up much of a fight because apparently the Government of Canada needs the free trade deal. How will the Prime Minister of our country ever be able to explain to Canadians why he received so little and gave away so much?
The Americans could not believe their good fortune. Here was a Government which was willing to give away all of its best bargaining chips, FIRA, the National Energy Program, even before the negotiations started. The Government has been willing during the course of these negotiations to sell out industry after industry. First it was our lumber industry, then our book and publishing industry and now it is the turn of the drug industry at the expense of the Canadian consumer.
On March 16 I asked in the House what would be next on the Tory sovereignty sell-out; oil and gas, steel, or potash? Potash is the next industry on the block. The preliminary decision of the United States to impose an 85 per cent countervailing duty on Canadian potash is the latest pressure tactic. That measure could wipe out the Saskatchewan industry. It could prevent Manitoba from getting in the game. It could wipe out the development in New Brunswick.
We expect the same "fearless" performance, to use the word of the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), whose great victory was to impose a 15 per cent export duty on our lumber industry at the request of the Americans, despite the fact that in 1983 we had won an identical case. Despite the fact that the underlying premises and facts had not changed, the Government of Canada lost its nerve and surrendered. It pleaded guilty before the trial and withdrew our case. The only difference between now and 1983 is that in 1983 we did not have a weak Government that was preoccupied with preserving a free trade deal at any cost.
I would advise the Canadian potash industry to be very wary of offers of help from the Minister for International Trade.
This Bill as proposed by the Government is bad legislation. It does not do what the Government states it will do in terms of research and development. It does not create more jobs. It does not give Canadians a new and larger variety of drugs. It only raises prices, and increases the profits of the multinationals.
Obviously the Government hopes that in the flurry of publicity that it has created by the incompetent handling of the refugee issue, Canadians will not notice that the real motive for recalling Parliament for this emergency session is to
pass this drug Bill. It is a cynical act by a desperate Government caving into the sovereign extraterritorial power of the United States.
I urge upon the House and the Minister a full consideration of the amendments that we proposed in the House, and the amendments proposed by the Senate and returned to us for reconsideration. These amendments would give a fair balance between research, jobs, and development on the one hand, and yet preserve stability in the drug price structure for the benefit of those Canadians least able to protect themselves; the aged, the chronically ill, the sick, the handicapped, those who cannot protect themselves and who depend upon Parliament to step up and call upon the Minister one last time before the end of the day to listen to reason and common sense, listen to the facts and the arguments, and be reasonable and accept our amendments.
Some Hon. Members; Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND-CONSIDERATION OF SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I, too, am very pleased to be able to make a few comments on this excellent Bill C-22.
A moment ago the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) referred to the few years' experience he had in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, of which he may have been the first Minister.
I, too, had this experience, Madam Speaker, and the opportunity to study in detail first the effects of the Liberal Party position on that project or the measures that date back to 1969, and particularly the Eastman project which was announced and launched in 1983. Madam Speaker, the Eastman Committee was set up precisely because the Party recognized that changes were needed. Changes were necessary because the evidence showed at the time that the existing legislation substantially reduced the number of jobs, and moreover, that it was causing a major outflow of the investments related to the pharmaceutical industry to other countries. Naturally, we all remember the most recent decision of this industry in Quebec when the Hoffmann-LaRoche company had to close down because of the inaction of the previous Government.
This is why it is important to make some changes. This is why we have introduced Bill C-22. First, because we firmly believe in the principle of protecting intellectual property. We believe that the time has come to align our patent rights on international practice, as patents are recognized throughout the world in all industrialized countries. To my knowledge, Canada is now virtually the only industrialized country where a company cannot always obtain patent rights for new drugs under the compulsory licencing system. To a certain extent, Canada is the only country where drug prices are controlled through intellectual property, and I believe that this must change.
August 26, 1987

If all countries had legislation as regressive as ours, no new drugs would ever be developed. Bill C-22 will bring back patent protection to a seven to ten year period, as we have already pointed out, and transform the Canadian pharmaceutical sector into a first-rate innovative industry, which will generate an important increase in investments and jobs in the area of research and development.
As it is, Madam Speaker, the Senate is not prepared to extend that kind of protection to our multinationals; naturally, they stand accused of making profits at the expense of consumers. But here is another point of view as expressed by columnist Lysiane Gagnon in the August 22 issue of La Presse, and I quote: "The major drug research laboratories are multinational companies. Why? Because applied research is very costly, of course. On average, they spend SI00 million over 10 years to develop and market a new drug, not to mention the time they waste working on risky ventures. No wonder there are no small- and medium-sized businesses or cooperatives in state-of-the-art research."
Well, Madam Speaker, our Senators would be quite satisfied with maintaining the status quo by granting drug manufacturers a four-year protection. The rationale underlying these amendments to the Patent Act is the creation of a climate likely to promote research and development in the drug industry. Indeed, as I said a moment ago, we want to stem the brain exodus towards foreign lands. Thousands of students, young researchers, and scientists are leaving Canada precisely because they cannot find jobs here and have much more challenging opportunities elsewhere.
1 also referred to the massive inflow of capital investments we can expect once Bill C-22 becomes law. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has been saying this everywhere: Canadians can look forward to investments in the order of $1.4 billion over a 10-year period, and this, I might add, in all regions of Canada, be it in Quebec, in Ontario where the main activities of the industry are located, or in the other provinces.
In 1995, research and development spending will total over $600 million annually. We must realize the impact this Bill will have on the future and health of Canadians. We must also remember that more than 30 per cent of the amounts to be spent on research and development will go to universities and research centres. The funds will also be used to coordinate our research and development efforts.
As I said earlier, every region in this country will benefit from the tremendous economic spin-offs. For instance, Nordic Laboratory in Montreal will receive $45 million. Universities and research centres in Edmonton and Calgary will receive $132 million. Hospitals and universities in Halifax and St. John's, Nefoundland, will receive $82 million. These are considerable amounts that will be distributed across our regions and benefit every Canadian who wants to dedicate his
Patent Act
energies and efforts to this work, as well as our young people in the regions.
However, in the other place, the Senate is proposing a fund that would total no more than $25 million, which money would be redistributed to the companies, not to universities and research centres.
Bill C-22 also means creating 3,000 jobs for scientists, as I mentioned earlier, jobs for researchers, jobs for young men and women, for young Canadian graduates. Over 1,200 jobs will be located in the province of Quebec. The protection provided under Bill C-22 for new drugs will not only benefit research and development, it will also expand the volume of manufacturing and exports in the Canadian drug industry.
As for generic drugs, it is said that the Bill will mean the end of the generic companies. Madam Speaker, our new policy will promote the manufacture of new generic products by making it attractive for the generic firms to manufacture the chemical ingredients used in the manufacture of drugs.
All import licences already granted to generic companies will be automatically converted to manufacturing licences. Generic companies will thus be able to manufacture the product directly. It is also very important to remember that all generic products now on the market will continue to be sold. When people say that Bill C-22 will increase the price of drugs, they are simply trying to fool Canadians. The impact of this Bill will certainly not be to increase the price of drugs. Generic companies will also be able to continue and expand their exports. Generic products represent only 7 per cent of the drugs sold in this country. So what happens to the 93 per cent that are not protected and are free game? That is why we want to create a price review board so that we can reassess and monitor the prices of these drugs, for the benefit of the consumer.
Now, Madam Speaker, Canada takes up only 2 percent of the world medicinal drugs market. Well, by favoring new investments, we will rank among such nations as Japan, Italy, the United States in terms of research investments, innovations and new technology development.
Canada, therefore, will be recognized as a country which welcomes investments, not only in the pharmaceutical industry, but also in many others.
If I may, Madam Speaker, I should like to mention that during 1986, Canada has experienced, in terms of foreign investments, its best year ever. Foreign investments in the order $6.8 billion have resulted in the creation of new jobs and fostered new investments, due clearly to a favourable economic climate and the new confidence which has taken hold of Canadian citizens and businessmen.
Again, Bill C-22 follows this philosophy which our Party adopted in 1984.

August 26, 1987
Patent Act
In the area of consumer protection, it should be emphasized that this policy, as I mentioned earlier, will continue to control the prices of drugs which are already sold in various drugstores, and to make sure that the future prices remain reasonable, there will be a fully independent Patent Medicine Prices Review Board which would be chaired by Dr. Eastman, the same man who carried out a study of the whole pharmaceutical industry. This organization will therefore be established.
Well, the Senate is against the creation of such a board and would rather entrust the control over the prices of these generic products to the free competition of the market-place.
Madam Speaker, that is not the way to protect Canadian consumers. As I said, 7 percent of patented medicine are subject to the competition of generic drugs. Canadians, therefore, have no way of knowing whether they are paying a fair price for the remaining 93 percent of these drugs when they are purchasing them.
So we are saying that the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board will review the price of all prescription drugs to provide that protection to consumers.
In formulating that policy, my Government has strived to reconcile the need to increase industrial research and development with the need to ensure the availability to Canadian people of pharmaceutical products at fair prices.
On the other hand, the report of the Senate committee means the status quo. Whatever means are used by the opposition and the Senate to present the matter in a misleading light, the only important thing for them is to obstruct the passage of the Bill.

Thank you, Madam Speaker, for again giving me a further opportunity to enter this debate over what the Government is attempting to do to a policy which has been seen by most Canadians as both fair and good for Canada.
Before I begin my few remarks I want to say to the Minister and government Members that in my view and that of many in Canada there is absolutely no consensus in this country which would encourage the Government to do what it has been attempting to do for the last year and several months. In fact, if there is a consensus in Canada it is that the Government should leave what has been a good policy for Canada and Canadian consumers as is.
1 want to say at the outset that the Government has absolutely no one to blame but itself for the fix it finds itself in today as between this House and the Senate. I say that because of the way this whole issue has been handled by the Government from day one. The entire process has been questionable. In that respect I think it would be useful to remind ourselves how Canada's present policy came about. It did not come about by a fluke or accident or mistake. It came about because of some very good, sound and solid reasons.
We must look at what the multinational drug companies were charging Canadian consumers for pharmaceutical products prior to 1969. It has been said time and time again, and the Government refuses to recognize it, that prior to 1969 Canadians were paying among the highest prices in the world for pharmaceutical products. It was because of those unacceptably high prices, and many called it price gouging at the time, that the Government of the day was forced to respond to the concerns expressed. The first response was in 1961 when the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission examined Canada's policy on pharmaceutical products and the price gouging that was going on. It studied the matter, heard witnesses, and concluded that the reason was that the multinational corporations held a monopoly on drug pricing in Canada. That commission was the first to recommend that the Canadian Government end that monopoly by removing patent protection on pharmaceutical products. The Government of the day did not respond to those recommendations.
The pressure still existed so again in 1963 Mr. Justice Emmett Hall headed a royal commission into the pricing of drugs. He came to the same conclusion; the reason drug prices were so high was because the companies enjoyed a monopoly in the market-place. He recommended that patent protection be removed from pharmaceutical products in order to force prices down.
As things very often go with Governments, no action was taken on those recommendations, probably because of the tremendous pressure being placed upon the Government by the multinational corporations. However, in 1967 the Government finally asked an all-Party House of Commons committee headed by a Conservative Member named Harley to study this. That House of Commons committee concluded the same as had every other study group, that there was a monopoly practice in place in Canada which was detrimental to the interests of Canadian consumers. It recommended to the Government of the day that patent protection be removed for pharmaceutical products.
After all those studies, commissions, debates in the House and public pressure, in 1969 the Government of the day finally removed patent protection for pharmaceutical products. That ended the monopoly on pricing structures which those multinational corporations had enjoyed up to that time. Interestingly enough, it permitted Canadian manufacturers, the so-called generic drug manufacturers or, as the Government likes to call them, copiers of drugs or burglars or thieves or whatever, to get into the field, pay the multinationals a 4 per cent royalty for the use of their drugs, and force Canadian drug prices down from the highest in the world prior to 1969 to among the lowest in the world today.
The multinational corporations have never accepted that policy since 1969. For years they not only pressured the Canadian Governments of the day to revert to patent protection but also hauled the generic drug manufacturers into the courts and dragged them through lengthy litigations. This has been well documented. It is not something I dreamed up. In many cases they made it so costly for the generic drug manufacturers to defend themselves in the courts that they were hopeful that they would drive them into bankruptcy and out of business. That has been well documented and has never been denied by the multinational corporations.
It is interesting to note that of all the cases the multinational corporations had before the courts they did not win one. Not one case was won by the multinationals. It was out and out harassment of those Canadian companies, primarily by American producers, that caused those legal actions.
The pressure was still on then as it is today. In 1981, the Economic Council of Canada reviewed Canada's policies and concluded, 12 years after the policy was adopted, that it was a good policy for Canadian consumers. That is another independent committee which made that judgment and those recommendations.
Later on, in 1981, the Canadian Institute for Public Policy did a further study of the pharmaceutical industry and concluded that Canada's policy was the correct one. Not satisfied with that, an internal committee of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs did its own study into
August 26, 1987

Canada's policy. That committee concluded that Canada's policy was a good one for Canadians.
As I said earlier, Madam Speaker, Governments being what they are, the Liberal Government of the day did not have the moral fortitude to tell the multinationals once and for all that the policy was good for Canadians and they should get lost. Instead it appointed Professor Harry Eastman to conduct yet another study into Canada's policy. We all know the results of that study. It is widely recognized, even by those who oppose his recommendations, that Professor Harry Eastman conducted the most intensive and thorough investigation into the pharmaceutical industry internationally.
After all of that, Professor Eastman tabled his report in the House of Commons, I believe in 1983. He concluded a number of things. For example, in 1983 alone, Canada's policy had saved Canadian consumers approximately $213 million on drug costs. He said that every previous commission recognized that a company should receive compensation for its efforts in developing a product. Those commissions concluded that the total cost to the pharmaceutical industry for research and development amounted to 4 per cent of total sales.
Therefore, Harry Eastman said, as previous commissions had, we should continue to pay the multinational companies 4 per cent royalties for all drugs copied by the generic drug manufacturers. He said as well that the approval process through the Department of National Health and Welfare to bring a new drug on the market was very cumbersome, and he made some recommendations on how that process could be speeded up. However, he said essentially that the policy should not be changed.
All of the studies since 1961 have recommended that Canada's policy should be as it is today. Therefore, why did the Government suddenly charge ahead, ignoring all these studies, the most recent one done in 1983, and introduce legislation through Bill C-22 which contains absolutely no reflection of the conclusions of all those studies?
One can conclude several things. The first conclusion is that it did so because of the tremendous pressure which was placed on Canada primarily by the multinational corporations based in the United States through President Reagan.
The Government denies that, but there is sufficient evidence available which clearly shows that that is the case. At the Shamrock Summit which took place in the Province of Quebec in 1985, President Reagan made that key demand as a prerequisite to agreeing to negotiations on a free trade package. That is the only reason we are faced with this legislation today. It is not to keep Canadian consumers happy but to satisfy a demand made by the President of the United States that a made-in-Canada policy for the benefit of Canadian consumers should be changed because he did not like it.
Regardless of the contents of this Bill, on that basis alone I would fight what the Government is trying to do. It is a direct

attack on the sovereignty of this nation and its right to make its own policies on behalf of Canadians. I find that totally offensive and I think most other Canadians do as well.
The Government has made much of the fact that there will be a prices review board established and that prices will not increase. It is stating that we are simply trying to scare Canadians. That is the usual rhetoric we hear from Governments when their position is extremely weak. They try to attack those who oppose the Bill.
It was not only I or other members of the New Democratic Party who said that. Professor Harry Eastman said that it would be extremely difficult for a prices review board to determine whether or not a drug company is charging too high a price once this legislation is passed by the House. There are a number of reasons for that assertion. Professor Eastman said:
A major problem with the price indexes for a large number of commodity groups is the difficulty in accounting for changes in quality of products.
This is an especially troublesome problem for the pharmaceutical industry in which, each year, several new products are introduced in the market-place as fairly direct competitors with an existing array of products.
He says:
-the price index does not capture any increase in the price of the new product relative to the old product even in those frequently encountered situations in which the old and the new drug have roughly the same therapeutic value to the prospective patient and thereby are, for practical purposes, the same product.
Eastman said further that separating out changes in the quality of a given drug is so exceedingly difficult that it is rarely accomplished. As a consequence, drug price changes "may inappropriately register changes in quality".
After he examined the situation even further, he said:
What is clear-is that the changes of price of particular products are not at all a satisfactory indicator of expenditure changes that have as their source decisions by the manufacturer. In addition to deciding on the price of particular products, the manufacturer can also quite clearly decide to introduce a new product that is therapeutically little different from the old product and, furthermore, can set a price for the new product significantly higher than that of the old product.
In other words, it is a common practice within the industry that a pharmaceutical drug that is intended to do a certain thing is marketed, and once the market is saturated, they simply change the fine chemicals in that drug, give it a new name, charge a higher price and market it under a different name. The two products are exactly the same but the company can jack up the price for the fine chemical change in the old product.
Another practice of the companies was referred to by my colleague, the Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), in a question to the Minister who spoke before me. It is referred to in some detail by a fellow named Stanley Adams in a book entitled Roche versus Adams. Stanley Adams was an employee in the pharmaceutical industry in the United Kingdom for many years. He was blackballed because

In conclusion, I do not think the prices review board will work. Every provincial Government in this country with the exception of one, I believe, have said that prices will increase at great detriment to consumers if this Bill goes through.
Affordable drugs are an integral part of our health care system in this country. The issue is not one of copying a mouse trap, as the Minister calls it when referring to intellectual property. If the Bill goes through it will make drugs much more expensive and, in my view, will weaken the medicare system in this country. Generic manufacturers point out that they must do their own R and D to meet Health Protection Branch regulations. They think a higher than 4 per cent figure could be justifiable, but no one has proved it to them yet. This is their position. The 4 per cent figure was set by the Commissioner of Patents on the first compulsory licence, and has not been varied since.
The Senate struggled with implementing particular amendments, after having had the full process of travelling across the country and in an unhurried fashion listening to witnesses.
If this were a wise Government, it would take a second look at the Bill and implement some of those proposals. It would receive some popularity in the country.
The conclusion must be that the Senate version of Bill C-22 is a better one than the one presented to the House. It allows the compulsory licensing system to work with far fewer impediments than the Government's Bill, and it presents a method of specific reward for companies based on actual research and development work undertaken. The Government's Bill simply offers the drug companies a massive blank cheque in the form of 10 years of exclusivity, whether or not they do the research and development. It has no sanctions for ensuring that the research and development investments are made. Therefore, that is why we oppose the Government's Bill, and would urge the Government to adopt some of the Senate amendments.
I wish to deal with the matter of research for a few minutes, because we keep hearing about all the research that is going on. The Senate version restores the emphasis on lower prices that the Government has sacrificed. It sought to make some guarantees that higher royalty payments to the brand name companies would actually result in research and development. It is interesting to note where the research is carried out. As I understand it, the real research in drug development is done in the home country of the large multinational drug companies, for example, in the United States or in Europe. The research that we get in Canada is limited research. It is market and clinical research, but it is not the type of deep research that the Government states it could be. There is much authority for that view. Many articles have been written.
A group called the Medical Reform Group of Ontario advised the House of Commons committee that it takes 200 to 300 people working at the same location to create a good centre for basic research, and that none of the pharmaceutical companies now operating in Canada has anywhere near that capacity. Therefore, there is not the capacity, plus it is not natural for them to do it in Canada. It is done at the home base of the multinational corporations.
The Minister stated in the House that $900 million would be invested. This is what one would call a form of boosterism and blackmail in order to have the House rush through with this Bill. I do not believe the argument on research.
The argument on jobs is an interesting one. The bait is that there will be 3,000 high-tech jobs for graduates. The Minister should look at the analysis of his own Department; it contradicts the Minister. Documents obtained by Southam News under the Access to Information Act illustrated that out of the magic number of 3,000, only 1,148 will be employed by the industry in a professional category. According to the documents, a further 541 will be employed extramurally, probably in universities and research institutes. A further 652 are classified as technical, which means lab technicians who could have an undergraduate or community college standing. There are 620 others who turn out to be, in the words of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, "Managers, cleaners, animal keepers, statisticians, and clerks". Therefore, the 3,000 high-tech, high quality jobs for Canadian scientists and biochemists over the next 10 years are not there. The companies plan to employ 1,148 professionals, or 38 per cent of what they have led people to believe.
One has to ask, what is the Government's real agenda? I think that the Government's real agenda is to make the United States happy and to remove this so-called trade irritant because that was part of the free trade deal. I listened to the question addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in the House, and he virtually has admitted as much. That is the Government's real agenda. It has an unpopular Bill. There are a small amount of people who are employed in the industry who naturally are in favour of the Bill. The public is not. Why would the public be in favour of a $400 million or $500 million increase in drug prices? Why would we go from some of the

As I said in the House last Thursday, I do not see why I should rely more on the promises of foreign multinationals that 1 rely on those of the Conservative Party which believes blindly that the foreign corporations will deliver the goods.
Yet, I understand the position of multinationals: they want a 10-year protection. However, to obtain such a long protection, they will try their utmost not to commit themselves. They do not want us to legislate here guarantees which would force them to carry out research in Canada. Clearly, if they can avoid that, surely they are not going to complain. On another level, perhaps less serious, they do not want to give guarantees in writing either. If they can avoid that, they will. We heard a few speeches, a few words that were spoken. But even that would never have come, had they not been forced to do so.
Our position is to give fangs, to give teeth to Bill C-22, in order to have the assurance that research will be done in this country, jobs will be created in Canada, especially in the Province of Quebec I am representing here. It is therefore a complete distortion of our position to suggest, as certain Members in this House have done, that we are against job creation in Quebec. Only clowns can say that.
The three political Parties agree when it comes to increasing research in Canada. The three Parties agree on creating new jobs in research. The difference is, some Parties are ready to accept at face value the promises made by companies that are not even established in Canada, that have their headquarters elsewhere, in foreign countries. Our position is very prudent. It is to say: You claim that you are going to do research, that you will be increasing the level of research-good, we want legislative guarantees to that effect. And if multinational corporations in the drug industry are sincere when they suggest they want to do research, I do not see why they would oppose an amendment that was put forward and that would cast in concrete that obligation to do research. And indeed Senators returned to the House of Commons the same amendment we put forward originally.
The problem is, why does the Government refuse to put its money where its mouth is? The Government says: We want those companies to do research in Canada. But when we say to the Government: Take the steps needed through a package of amendments that is already there, amendments to ensure that this will happen, the Government's answer is: No, pass the Bill as it is. In short, the Government is telling us it is trusting foreign companies. Perhaps there are other reasons. Why is the Government rejecting that amendment? Is it under pressure from those multinational corporations that say: Look here, the Opposition is getting tired, they have been talking for a long

August 26, 1987

time, in the end they will let it pass. Do not accept that amendment. Have no fear, we will do research. Were the American authorities themselves under pressure? We all know about the lobbying system in the United States, and 1 am not blaming the multinationals with headquarters in the United States for putting pressure on the American politicians and asking them to speak to us about it, because the Americans are well aware that the Prime Minister and the Conservative Party have promised to deliver a free trade agreement and must now do so as the Canadian Government would look rather silly if the free trade negotiations fell through. This is a pressure point or a lever which the American Government can use, and this might be one of the reasons why this Government refuses to accept an amendment which is otherwise extremely reasonable. When you want something to happen, you do whatever is necessary to ensure that it does. If not, you are faced with the present situation where the Government does not practice what it preaches. The Government says that it wants research and jobs, but when we suggest that it take the necessary action, it refuses to do so. I am beginning to wonder whether the Government is sincere in its desire to have more research activities carried out in Canada.
Madam Speaker, you do not have to be in politics for long to know that we have students in our universities who are learning how to do scientific research for the future. They chose science because they have the ability and the desire required and know that they will have stable and well-paid jobs. You do not need a dictionary to learn that. You do not need to have been a Member of Parliament for 20 years to understand that anyone who objected to this would not be reelected.
I therefore believe that the Government is going far enough today by imposing closure without repeating the nonsense that Liberals are opposed to research and job creation, as though Canadians could be so stupid as to believe that the politicians would have the idiocy of telling people that they do not want them to have jobs.

We did not tell the Government that we had changed our mind, that overnight we had come to appreciate the full value of Bill C-22; we said that we had debated the measure, that we got our message across and made our views clear, and that we were prepared to vote as soon as our leader would have addressed the House.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member's remarks, especially at they concerned the Senate royalty fund.
I do not think he understands what he is talking about. According to page 365 of the Eastman Commission of Inquiry report, the royalty fund as proposed by the Senate would have raised $4.6 million for research in 1983. That is a substantial amount, but does not compare with the $1.4 billion that we will raise the other way.
The fund would have meant a cost to consumers of $30.6 million because of increased drug prices resulting from higher royalties. Over 10 years, using the same methodology, the total cost to consumers would have been $700 million to $1.1 billion.
When one considers another aspect, the Senate's proposal does not include a drug prices review board. There is no protection for consumers against these added costs. On the other hand, the drug prices review board as proposed by the Government, and supported by many different people, including officials in the Saskatchewan pharmacare program, is expected to save consumers hundreds of millions of dollars over the same time period.
The only conclusion I can reach is that the Senate's proposals are far more detrimental to the consumer than the Government's legislation. They come nowhere near the economic benefits of Bill C-22. How can the Hon. Member justify the Senate royalty fund raising $4.6 million for research at a cost of $30.6 million in increased drug prices? It
August 26, 1987

does not make sense to me. It may be Liberal philosophy, but it sure is not ours,

Madam Speaker, I will start with the second question. The Hon. Member asks why there is no price review mechanism in our position. It is simple to understand. There is no need for it. When one shortens the period of exclusivity and allows generic companies to begin copying the drug and retailing it at a lower cost after four years instead of ten years, the prices are kept down. Look at the experience in Canada when the period of exclusivity was removed and generics began copying and distributing at half the price. Prices went down. That is not difficult to understand.
Why would we agree with a price review mechanism that is proposed in Bill C-22 when it is only a review? There are no roll-back provisions.

Our proposal will make sure that prices do not go up. Therefore, there would be no need for a mechanism to try to push them down.

Madam Speaker, does the Hon. Member believe that we have had a fair debate on Bill C-22 in the House, considering the fact that at second reading, which was ended by time allocation, there were four occasions on which we spoke to the Bill? They were November 20, November 21, November 24 and November 25, for a total of 11 hours and five minutes. There was a total of 26 speakers, and time allocation was moved after only five speakers had spoken.
In committee, this Bill had 13 sessions with witnesses. Fifty groups were heard, with a 45-minute time limit. The Government severely limited the number of witnesses who could be heard. It dropped the offer to travel to other parts of Canada and rejected the possibility of having American witnesses who could testify about the American experience without generic drug legislation.
At report stage, this Bill was ended by time allocation after 10 hours and 12 minutes, and after only two out of 11 groups of amendments had been dealt with.
Third reading of this Bill was ended by time allocation and our Party, for example, only had two Members who were able to address the issue at third reading.
